content: The World Health Organization (WHO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations (UN) that serves as the leading authority on international public health. It was established on April 7, 1948, and is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. The WHO inherited its mandate and resources from the Health Organization, which was part of the League of Nations. The WHO's constitution defines its primary objective as achieving the highest possible level of health for all people. Its core mission includes combating diseases, particularly infectious diseases, and promoting overall global health. The organization was formally established on the first World Health Day, April 7, 1948, when its constitution was ratified by the 26th member state. Before this, its functions were managed by an Interim Commission following the International Health Conference in 1946. The WHO coordinates international efforts to monitor and respond to infectious disease outbreaks, such as SARS, malaria, and AIDS. It also sponsors programs aimed at preventing and treating these diseases. The organization supports the development and distribution of safe and effective vaccines, diagnostics, and medications. Notably, after more than two decades of effort, the WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980, marking the first disease eliminated through human intervention. The WHO is also working on vaccines for malaria and schistosomiasis and aims to eradicate polio in the near future. In 2006, the WHO endorsed the first official HIV/AIDS Toolkit for Zimbabwe, setting an international standard. Beyond disease eradication, the WHO conducts health campaigns, such as promoting fruit and vegetable consumption and discouraging tobacco use. In February 2007, experts at WHO headquarters reported significant progress in developing pandemic influenza vaccines, with over 40 clinical trials completed or ongoing. These trials, initially focused on healthy adults, have expanded to include children and the elderly, with all vaccines showing safety and tolerability across age groups. The WHO also engages in research on controversial topics, such as the potential health effects of electromagnetic fields from cell phones. For example, a 2003 joint WHO/FAO report recommended limiting sugar intake to less than 10% of total energy in a healthy diet. This recommendation faced opposition from the sugar industry, but the WHO/FAO stood by its findings based on scientific evidence. The WHO has additional responsibilities under international treaties, such as the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs and the Convention on Psychotropic Substances. These treaties require the WHO to provide scientific and medical assessments of psychoactive drugs and recommend their regulation. The organization also publishes the International Classification of Diseases (ICD), with the 10th revision released in 1992 and later updates available online and in print. The WHO maintains a model list of essential medicines that all healthcare systems should provide affordably. The WHO's governance structure includes the World Health Assembly, its supreme decision-making body, which meets annually in May. All UN member states are eligible for WHO membership, and the organization currently has 193 member states. The Assembly elects the Director-General every five years and appoints 34 health experts to the Executive Board for three-year terms. The Executive Board implements Assembly decisions, advises the Assembly, and facilitates its work. The WHO's funding comes from member state contributions and donations from various sources, including NGOs, the pharmaceutical industry, and foundations like the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. Voluntary contributions now exceed assessed contributions from member states. The WHO operates six regional offices, each with significant autonomy. These offices are led by Regional Directors, elected for five-year terms, and oversee health policies and programs within their regions. The regional offices are located in Brazzaville (Africa), Copenhagen (Europe), New Delhi (South-East Asia), Cairo (Eastern Mediterranean), Manila (Western Pacific), and Washington, D.C. (Americas). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the regional office for the Americas, predates the WHO and is the most autonomous. The WHO also maintains 147 country and liaison offices worldwide. These offices, typically located in national capitals, are led by WHO Representatives, who are trained physicians with diplomatic rank. The country offices advise governments on health and pharmaceutical policies and serve as the WHO's primary presence in member states. The WHO collaborates with private sector initiatives, such as the Program for Appropriate Technology in Health (PATH), the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI), and the Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV), among others. These partnerships focus on developing vaccines, diagnostics, and treatments for neglected diseases. The WHO has had several notable Directors-General and associated figures, including epidemiologists and public health experts. The organization has also implemented policies to promote a tobacco-free work environment, including a ban on hiring cigarette smokers. The WHO publishes the annual World Health Report, which provides expert assessments of global health and focuses on specific topics. The report is a key resource for health statistics and policy-making. The WHO has faced controversies, such as its relationship with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Critics argue that an agreement between the two organizations, established in 1959, limits the WHO's ability to address health effects of ionizing radiation. For example, the WHO's reports on the Chernobyl disaster have been criticized for underestimating its health impacts. Protests against this agreement have been ongoing since 2007.
